chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ibn Mahbub, from Abu Ayyub, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said:

'When the menstruating woman intends to perform ghusl, let her insert a piece of cotton. If something of blood comes out in it, she should not perform ghusl; but if she sees nothing, let her perform ghusl. And if she sees yellowness after that, let her perform wudu and pray.'

key_terms.الْحَائِضُ: the menstruating woman — a woman in the state of hayd (menstruation), during which certain acts of worship are suspended
key_terms.تَغْتَسِلَ: to perform ghusl — the major ritual bath required for purification after menstruation (hayd) ends
key_terms.صُفْرَةً: yellowness (sufra) — a discharge that may appear at the end of menstruation; considered legally minor, requiring only wudu rather than ghusl
key_terms.قُطْنَةً: a piece of cotton — used as an internal check to determine whether menstrual blood has fully ceased

ai.seo_question: How does a menstruating woman determine when it is permissible to perform ghusl according to Imam al-Baqir?
ai.summary: This hadith from Imam al-Baqir (AS) provides a practical method for a menstruating woman to verify the cessation of her menses before performing the ritual bath (ghusl). The ruling is precise: if blood is still present, ghusl is premature; if no blood is found, ghusl is valid; and if only yellowness (sufra) appears after ghusl, a lesser purification (wudu) suffices for prayer. This teaching reflects the meticulous attention to purity (tahara) in Islamic jurisprudence, where the distinction between blood and non-blood discharge determines the type of purification required.
